title: ISACA CGEIT
summary: Certified in the Governance of Enterprise IT (CGEIT) is an ISACA certification for experienced professionals who direct, manage and assure information technology (IT) from a governance point of view. It sits at a senior level and suits IT managers, risk and compliance leads, auditors, architects and consultants who already hold responsibility for how technology serves business goals. It proves to an employer that you can shape an IT governance framework, manage IT resources and risk, and measure whether IT is delivering value. The exam is multiple choice and covers five domains, and ISACA also expects qualifying work experience. Typical roles after certification include IT governance manager, IT risk manager, enterprise architect and audit director. This is an independent study guide that is not official ISACA material; check the vendor's current version before booking.

beginner.definition: Certified in the Governance of Enterprise IT (CGEIT) is an ISACA certification about running technology in a controlled way. It is not a hands on technical exam. It is for people who decide how technology should be used, funded and checked in a company.
beginner.whyItMatters: Companies spend large amounts of money on technology. Leaders must show that this spending is planned, safe and useful. This certificate proves you can set up that control system. It is often asked for in senior roles, such as IT governance manager or audit director. It also helps you talk to business leaders and not only to engineers.
howItWorks: Read the official ISACA exam outline and note the five domains and their share of the exam.
Study common governance ideas, such as direction setting, monitoring and assurance.
Learn one widely used framework, for example Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies (COBIT).
Study how organisations assess and treat technology risk, and how they measure value.
Practise questions that describe a business problem and ask for the best management action.
The exam is multiple choice, and it expects you to choose the answer that fits governance best, not the most technical fix.
beginner.example: Imagine a bank that wants to move its customer system to the cloud. The engineers can list the technical steps. The governance question is different. Who approves the spend, what happens if the supplier fails, how do we measure success, and who reports back to the board? A CGEIT holder is the person who designs those rules before the first server moves. That is why the exam asks about decisions and control, not about server settings.
takeaways: CGEIT is a senior certification, so it makes most sense after several years of IT or audit work.
The exam rewards the answer that fits good governance, even when a clever technical fix is offered.
Learn one governance framework well instead of skimming several at once.

objectives: Explain how an enterprise governance of IT framework is set up in a real organisation
Describe the duties of a board and of senior management when they direct technology
Assess and treat technology risk in line with the organisation's risk appetite
Plan and manage technology resources, including people, money and suppliers
Define measures that show whether technology is delivering business value
Judge how new technology and regulation change an existing governance approach

chapters.title: Governance of enterprise IT
objectives: Describe the difference between governance, management and day to day operations
Set up decision rights so that technology choices are made by the right people
Align the technology plan with the business strategy and its goals
Build a governance framework using recognised standards such as Control Objectives for Information and Related Technologies (COBIT)
Report governance results to the board in clear business language

chapters.title: IT resources
objectives: Plan the technology workforce, including skills, roles and succession
Prepare and control an IT budget that supports agreed business aims
Manage outsourcing and supplier relationships through the whole contract
Assess the quality and fitness of data used for business decisions
Support change and transformation without breaking current services

chapters.title: Benefits realisation
objectives: Write a business case that states the expected benefits in measurable terms
Choose measures and key performance indicators that prove value was delivered
Track a project portfolio and stop work that no longer earns its place
Report benefit delivery honestly, including when targets are missed
Review benefits after a project ends and feed the lessons into the next one

chapters.title: Risk optimisation
objectives: Identify and score technology risk using a repeatable method
Set out risk appetite and tolerance in terms that staff can apply
Select risk responses such as avoid, reduce, share or accept
Link technology risk to enterprise risk and to legal duties
Monitor risk over time and report changes that need a decision

chapters.title: Resource optimisation
objectives: Review the technology estate and remove duplicated or unused services
Balance cost, performance and service quality in resourcing choices
Plan capacity and skills so that demand can be met
Use sourcing options such as in house teams, managed services or cloud
Measure the efficiency of technology delivery and act on the results
